# Data
Load libraries
```{r}
pacman::p_load(sf, # spatial
               here, 
               tidyverse, 
               rio, # for importing
               GWmodel # geographically weighted regression functions
               )
```

Read in shapefiles
```{r}
## Read in case shapefile - TIRS_SINAVE_22_23
cases <- st_read(dsn = here("data"), 
                 layer = "TIRS_SINAVE_22_23")
## Cluster shapefile
clusters <- st_read(dsn = here("data"),
                    layer = "Cluster final 2021 actualizado")
```

# Mapping

## What We Have

Our shapefiles include

- .dbf file: contains attribute table

- .shp file: contains track outlines

- .shx file: connective tissue to link it all together

- .prj file: for map projection

- .cpg file: used to specify the code page to identify character encoding

The two shapefiles are for the cluster polygons (From David, actual lifesaver)
and the cases.

## What I'd Like to do
Plot and see at what level cases are clustering -- household? block? cluster?

## Data Exploration, Learning GIS

### Cluster Map

#### Plot Only Clusters
```{r}
plot(clusters['CLUSTER'],
     col = adjustcolor("grey", alpha=0.5),
     lwd = 0.3)
```

#### Plot by TIRS Arm
```{r}
plot(clusters['TIRS'],
     pal = c("tomato", "darkolivegreen2"),
     lwd = 0.3)
```

### Cases Map (by Year)
```{r}
plot(cases["Year"],
     pal = c("pink", "cadetblue3"))
```

## ggplot Full Map
```{r}
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = clusters, linewidth = 0.05, aes(fill = as.factor(TIRS))) +
  geom_sf(data = cases, size = 0.2, stroke = 0,
          aes(color = as.factor(Year))) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("tomato", "darkolivegreen2"), 
                    name = "TIRS", labels = c("No", "Yes")) + 
  guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3))) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("lightblue", "navy"), 
                    name = "Year", labels = c("2022", "2023")) +
  theme_minimal()
ggsave("case_clusters.pdf")
```

```{r, include=FALSE}
# Finding limits for zooming in:
print(clusters, n = 2)

# X cut points:
by_x <- (234607.3 - 219180.1) / 8
x_coord <- seq(219180.1, 234607.3, by = by_x)

# plotting
for (i in 1:(length(x_coord)-1)){

    plot <- ggplot() +
      geom_sf(data = clusters, linewidth = 0.1, aes(fill = as.factor(TIRS))) +
      geom_sf(data = cases, size = 1,
              aes(color = as.factor(Year))) +
      scale_fill_manual(values = c("tomato", "darkolivegreen2"),
                        name = "TIRS", labels = c("No", "Yes")) +
      scale_color_manual(values = c("black", "lightblue", "navy"), 
                        name = "Year", labels = c("2022", "2023", "houses")) +
      coord_sf(xlim = c(x_coord[i], x_coord[i+1]), 
               ylim = c(y_coord[j], y_coord[j+1])) +
      theme_minimal()
    
    print(plot)
  }
}
```

### model

Want to fit a geographically weighted regression to see the relationship between cases and intervention ? 

Outcome: symptomatic Aedes-borne disease cases
Covariates: TIRS intervention, (mosquito density) ?????
Potential confounders: sociodemographic data

from module:
Now we are ready to fit *geographically weighted regression* (GWR).  GWR uses weighting to fit local regression values to allow the slopes associated with each covariate to change (smoothly) over space.  (See Lecture notes for details).  To estimate the association $\beta(s)$ for a location $s$, GWR uses kernel weights (similar to our intensity estimation for point process data) to weight observations (outcomes and covariates) near $s$ more to give an estimate of $\beta$ associated with location $s$. If you move over, the weights change and the estimated association ($\beta$).   The kernels make sure that if you don't move far, the estimate doesn't change much so we get a smooth surface for $\beta$.

We do this in two steps.  

First, we estimate the bandwidth for the kernel using cross validation (CV).

Next, we use the estimated bandwidth to fit the Poisson GWR model.

```{r}
# fitting poisson geographically weighted regression ??


### Now to fit Poisson GWR!
# The function 'ggwr' in the 'spgwr' package uses syntax similar to 'glm'
# (like we would use in a standard Poisson regression).
# 'longlat' tells the function that our coordinates are in longitude and
# latitude coordinates.
# 'ggwr.sel' selects the bandwidth for GWR based on the data, the model,
# and cross-validation
# Create distance matrix from centroids

houston.sp <- houston %>%
  as('Spatial')
DM <- gw.dist(dp.locat = coordinates(houston.sp))
head(houston)
houston.bw <- bw.gwr(violence_2 ~ Zl_total + Zl_drug + offset(log(POP2000)),
             data = houston.sp, 
             adaptive=TRUE, 
             dMat=DM)

bgwr <- ggwr.basic(violence_2 ~ Zl_total + Zl_drug + offset(log(POP2000)), 
                      data =houston.sp,
                      family = "poisson",
                      bw = houston.bw, 
                      kernel = "bisquare", 
                      adaptive = TRUE,
                      dMat = DM)
```
